**[p. 12]** In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah al-‘Alaq (The Clot)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created.﴾ ﴿He created man from a clot.﴾ ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous.﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen.﴾ ﴿Taught man what he did not know.﴾

In these five verses there are nine issues, some of which are linked to others in the relation of cause and effect (*sabab* and *musabbab*), of the general and the particular (*‘amm* and *khass*), and of the proof and what it proves. All of them belong to the method of this blessed Book. In reality, they are all fundamental issues of great importance and great significance.

Ibn Taymiyyah said about them: "They, and others like them among the surahs, contain wonders, because of what they establish as the opening of that great message. You cannot give them their due, due to incapacity and shortcoming."

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah wrote about them in his own style two hundred and twenty consecutive pages, and a further section on topics related to them. If we were to include everything we could, it would go beyond the subject of this book. Therefore we limit our discussion to what relates to its subject, except for what the pen has run over that cannot be left out. Success is from Allah, exalted is He.

As for the nine issues mentioned here, we present them so that we may be guided by them. They are:

First: The command to read, addressed to an unlettered Prophet.

Second: That this reading is in the name of the Lord, glorified is He, with the name being attributed to the addressee, ﷺ, as in *"in the name of your Lord."*

Third: A description of the Lord as "the One who created," in place of the name Allah, or the name "the One who gives life and causes death," or other than that.

Fourth: The creation of man specifically, after the generality of creation and its absoluteness.

**[p. 13]** Fifth: ﴿He created man from a clot.﴾ It does not mention what comes before the clot, such as a drop of semen, or the creation of Adam from dust.

Sixth: The repetition of the command to read along with ﴿and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾, in place of any other attribute, and in place of "the One who created," which was mentioned earlier.

Eighth: Teaching by the pen.

Ninth: Teaching man what he did not know.

* *

Since this surah is the first surah revealed of the Qur'an, and those five verses were, according to the correct view, the first part of it to be revealed, they are truly the opening of revelation. They have been the focus of the attention of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) and others, and discussion of this is extensive in the books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), hadith and the biography of the Prophet. So there is no reason to repeat it here. But we will present the discussion of what we have mentioned of the subject of this book, if Allah wills.

As for the first issue: His saying, exalted is He, *iqra'* (read). Linguistically, *qira'ah* (reading) means manifestation and bringing forth, as it was said in describing the she-camel: *lam taqra' janinan*, meaning she did not bring forth a fetus.

The Shaykh had previously explained this linguistic meaning, and directing the command to read to an unlettered Prophet involves no contradiction. This is because reading may be from something written, and it may be from something recited. Here it is from something recited, which Jibril, peace be upon him, recites to him. This is a greater manifestation of the miracle, because the one who was unlettered yesterday has become a teacher today. The context has indicated these two types of reading, since it combines reading with teaching by the pen.

In His saying, exalted is He, *iqra'* (read), there is a beginning of prophethood and an indication of the message, because he is reading the words of another.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, confirms this indication, meaning: it is not from you, nor from Jibril who is reading to you.

We have previously refuted the claim that he, ﷺ, did not write and could not read what was written, on the grounds that this protects the message, just as he did not compose poetry, nor was that appropriate for him; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted.

As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿You did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand, for then would the falsifiers have doubted.﴾ [al-‘Ankabut: 48]. That was in the context of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses.﴾ [al-Jumu‘ah: 2].

**[p. 14]** Here He did not specify what he reads. But the coming of Surah al-Qadr after it serves as an explanation of what he reads, which is: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. And the explanation of what was sent down comes in Surah al-Dukhan: ﴿Ha-Mim. By the clear Book. Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 1–3].

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and on us, has an explanation of this when he comments on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa’: 113]. So it is as if it means: "Read what is revealed to you from your Lord." What is meant by it is the Qur'an, by consensus (*ijma‘*).

* *

The second issue: His saying, ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, meaning: read in the name of your Lord, beginning and initiating the reading in the name of your Lord. The exegetes have discussed whether the *ba’* (in) is *silah* (a connecting particle, i.e. redundant), so that the sense would be *iqra' ismu rabbika* (read the name of your Lord), meaning: say "in the name of Allah," as at the beginning of the surahs.

It was also said: the *ba’* means *‘ala* (upon), meaning: upon the name of your Lord. In this case, the object of reading is omitted.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that His saying ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾ means that what you read is from your Lord, and you convey it to people in the name of your Lord, and you are a conveyer on behalf of your Lord, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed.﴾ [al-Najm: 3–4].

And His saying: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾ [al-Ma’idah: 99], meaning: from Allah, exalted is He.

And like His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by permission of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa’: 64].

A parallel to this in the present-day conventions is the address of the authority, or what is called the "throne address," when the one who delivers it says "in the name of the King," or "in the name of the nation," or "in the name of the people," according to the system of the state, meaning in the name of the authority from which the source of legislation and political direction comes.

Here it is "in the name of Allah, in the name of your Lord." The attribute "your Lord" here carries the meaning of lordship (*rububiyyah*), which alerts the servant to what Allah has bestowed upon him of nurture, care and attention. For the Lord does for His servant what sets him right, and part of the perfection of His setting him right is that He sends to him one who recites to him His revelation, with the news of this world and the Hereafter. And attributing it to the addressee is an act of comforting him.

* *

The third issue: the description of the Lord as ﴿who created﴾ together with the absolute form of the attribute. This is because the attribute of creation is the closest of the attributes to the meaning of lordship, and because it is the most comprehensive of the attributes for making Allah, exalted is He, known to His creation, and it is the attribute that they accept: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: Allah﴾ [Luqman: 25].

**[p. 15]** ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: Allah﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87].

And because every created thing must have a creator: ﴿Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35]. He has left the attribute of creation absolute, without mention of any created thing, so that it covers and includes all existence: the Creator of everything, in His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things﴾ [al-An‘am: 102]. ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs﴾ [al-Zumar: 62]. ﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾ [al-Hashr: 24].

These three issues are the foundations of the message, and what follows is evidence for them. The command to read is an obligation to bear revelation, the phrase "in the name of your Lord" is a clarification of the direction of the obligation, and "who created" is a proof of that direction, that is, of the message, the messenger and the one who sends, together with the general evidence. There is no doubt that those to whom he was sent did not believe in any one of them, so it was necessary to establish proofs for their confirmation in detail.

* *

Since the direction of the sender is the basis and the source, the proof for it came first, and the detail concerning it came with what they accept and what they accept in themselves. This is the fourth issue.

The fifth: ﴿He created man from a clot.﴾ This is a detail after a general statement, an explanation of a part of the whole, since man is a part of what He created. The mention of it is from mentioning the general after the specific at first, and from holding them to what they accept, and then moving them from what they know and admit to what they do not know and deny.

Mentioning man after the generality of creation is an honouring of him, like the mention of the Spirit after the generality of the angels: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4] and similar. Here "man" refers to the species, as evidenced by the plural in *‘alaq*, which is the plural of *‘alaqah*. And also because it is clearer in demonstrating the point to them, so that they may draw inference from themselves, as will come later.

His saying: *min ‘alaq* (from a clot). *‘Alaq* is the plural of *‘alaqah*, which is a piece of blood, like a thread or a strand. It is an explanation of His power, exalted is He. This is because they witness this sometimes in what the womb expels, and they know that it is the origin of the creation of man.

**[p. 16]** So the One who is able to bring a human being into the best of forms from this clot is able to make you a reader, even though you did not know reading before. Just as He brought man into existence from that clot when he had not existed before. And because the One who looks after that clot until it becomes a complete human being looks after you with the message.

And it may be that choosing man specifically, and in particular, to detail the stage of his existence, is because the other created beings do not know the beginnings of their creation as they know about man. And because man was mentioned earlier in the surah before it: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4]. So He made clear that from this clot he was in the best of stature, and part of the best of stature is the sending down of the upright Book.

Ibn Taymiyyah said: "The context here is one of proof for the existence of Allah. So He began with what they know and accept about Allah, and He did not begin with the drop of semen or with the dust. This is because the creation of Adam from dust was not witnessed by them, and because the drop of semen is not necessarily followed by the creation of man, since it may be ejected outside a womb as in the case of one who has had a wet dream, and it may be in a womb and yet not form into a human. Ended."

This in itself is sound. But it is not far-fetched to say: the surah is at the very beginning and onset of revelation. It is like one who says: "If I have begun the revelation to him and it was not there before, and nothing of it existed in relation to you, then it is no more remarkable than the creation of man from a clot, after he was nothing."

On this basis it may be said: the stage of the drop of semen has been set aside in correspondence with a stage of revelation, which has also been set aside, namely the period of the good dream. As in the two *Sahih*s: "The first thing with which revelation began for the Prophet ﷺ was the good dream; he would see it, and it would come like the break of dawn." So that was a preparation for prophethood and a groundwork for it, for a period of six months. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "The good dream is seen by the righteous man, or is seen for him, as one part of forty-six parts of prophethood." This is the ratio of half a year to the twenty-three years of the period of revelation. But the good dream may be seen by a righteous man, and in exactly the same way the drop of semen: there may be a drop of semen without there being a human being, just as there may be a dream without there being prophethood. As for the clot, it exists only in a womb and a firm resting place, and from there the human comes out fully formed, or not formed, according to what is decreed for him.

Since the stage of the drop of semen is not necessary for the creation of man, and the stage of the dream similarly is not necessary for prophethood, each of them has been set aside in correspondence with the other. The proof begins with what is the actual reality accepted by all, that Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator, and the Creator of man from a clot. Thus it involves establishing proof from the very selfhood of the one who reasons, **[p. 17]** so the proof is the creation of man, and what is taken as evidence is man himself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. So he reasons from his own self to the power of his Creator, glorified is He.

* *

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 96, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

When this argument for the power of the Creator Lord has been completed, there follows the establishment of proof for the validity of prophethood and the message of the Messenger (ﷺ). Thus comes the sixth issue, which is the repetition of the reading in His words: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾, since He has established the proof that you are sent from Allah, conveying from Him and reciting in His name. Know that this reading and this revelation are from your Lord, the Most Generous. The scholars have said that al-Akram (the Most Generous) is the One who gives without return and without expecting return. In reality, the coming of this attribute here, al-Akram, instead of any other attribute, is because of the harmony this attribute has with the context, which no other attribute would suit in its place, due to the greatness of the gift and the abundance of the favour.
First: the mercy to creation through this reading, which connected the servants to their Lord. That is sufficient.
Second: the blessing of creation and bringing into existence, for these are two complementary blessings: bringing into existence from non-existence through creation, and the second bringing into existence from ignorance to knowledge. None of this occurs except from the Lord, the Most Generous, glory be to Him.
* *
Then comes the eighth issue, which is among the indications of prophethood and message: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾. Whether the pause is at "Read" and the new sentence begins: "And your Lord is the Most Generous, Who taught by the pen";
or the pause is at "the Most Generous" and the new sentence begins: "Who taught by the pen"; because whoever teaches the ignorant by the pen, teaches others without the pen, by the common factor of teaching after ignorance. So the One able to do this is able to do that.
* *
The ninth: an explanation of this generality, since it did not specify what He taught by the pen. So He said: "He taught man what he did not know," and this is observed and tangible in their persons: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [an-Nahl: 78].
So Allah is the One who taught man what he did not know, and everything man has learned is from Allah: ﴿You teach them of what Allah has taught you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]. And is prophethood and messagehood anything other than the Messenger's being taught what he did not know? By this, the establishment of proof for the validity of prophethood is complete, that is, of the message, the Messenger and the one sent, and these are the foundations of the new call and mission.
It is well known among people that he was given prophethood with "Read" and was sent with "al-Muddaththir." But within this very surah there is the meaning of messagehood, because of what we have presented: that reading in the name of your Lord is an indication that he is sent from his Lord to those to whom he recites. Thus in it is the affirmation of messagehood from the very beginning of the revelation.

**Admonition**

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾, there is a topic of teaching and a question arises. If Allah, exalted is He, praised Himself by saying that He taught by the pen, and that He taught man what he did not know, then this contains an elevation of the status of the pen, since Allah, exalted is He, taught by means of it. This is the highest degree of honour, even though He, glorified is He, is capable of teaching without the pen. Then He mentioned it in the context of honouring it, in His saying: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 1-2]. The greatness of what is sworn to, which is Allah's grace upon His Messenger ﷺ through revelation, indicates the greatness of what is sworn by, which is the pen and what they inscribe with it of the writing of revelation and other things.

The pen has been mentioned in the Sunnah in various kinds, all of which are of the utmost importance.

Among them, the first and highest of them is:

The pen that wrote what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection. What is reported in the hadith is: "The first thing Allah created was the pen, and He said to it: 'Write!'" [the hadith].

So according to the narration with the marfu' (raised) form, it is the first of the created things, and then the whole of the decree proceeded, and everything whose existence was decreed.

Second: the pen that writes the destinies of the year on the Night of Power each year, indicated by His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4].

Third: the pen with which the angel writes in the womb what pertains to the servant of provision and deeds.

Fourth: the pen that is in the hands of the Noble Scribes, referred to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], meaning by writing, as in His saying: ﴿Noble, writing down﴾ ﴿knowing what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 11-12], if we say that writing in that requires a pen, as is apparent.

Fifth: the pen that is in the hands of people, with which they write what Allah teaches them. Among the most important of these are the pens of the scribes of revelation, who used to write the revelation in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the writing of Sulayman to Bilqis.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ encompasses all of this, since all of this is the matter of the pen and the greatness of its affair, and the great favour bestowed through it upon the Ummah, indeed upon the whole of creation.

The Message began with reading and writing. So why was the Prophet ﷺ, who announced all this virtue of the pen, not himself a writer with it, nor one of its people? Rather he was unlettered, neither reading nor writing, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2].

The answer is: we have first pointed to one aspect of it, which is that it is more complete as a miracle, since the unlettered Prophet became a teacher, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He recites to them His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164].

Second: this unlettered Prophet did not neglect the matter of the pen; rather he gave it the fullest care. The first and greatest of this is that he took scribes of revelation who wrote what was revealed to him in his presence, although he himself memorised and preserved it. Allah took on the guarantee of preserving and safeguarding it for him in His saying: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'la: 6-7]. Even what he forgets, Allah compensates him with something better than it or like it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better than it or the like of it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. Allah, exalted is He, promised to preserve it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

Nevertheless, he used to command that this preserved matter be written down, and he had a number of scribes. This is the utmost in care for the pen.

Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned among the scribes the four Caliphs, and together with them the remainder of seventeen persons. Then the Prophet ﷺ did not limit his care for the pen and teaching by it to the writing of revelation; rather he made teaching by it more general. As the report of 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As came: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded him to teach the people writing in Madinah, and he was a skilled scribe." This was mentioned by the author of al-Taratib al-Idariyya, from Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Isti'ab.

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I taught some people from the People of the Suffah (ahl al-Suffah) writing and the Qur'an."

The Prophet's ﷺ call to kings to Islam was by writing, as is well known.

Even further than this is what came in the account of the captives of Badr, where he ransomed with wealth whoever was able to pay the ransom, and whoever was not able to pay, and who knew writing, his ransom was that he teach ten of the boys writing. Thus writing became widespread in Madinah after that.

Among those who learned was Zayd ibn Thabit and others.

If the Muslims, in the early stage of their affair and in the greatest need of wealth and weapons, and even the enslaving of captives, put the teaching of boys writing before all of that, this indicates two matters:

The first of them: the intensity and increase of care for teaching.

The second of them: the permissibility of a disbeliever teaching a Muslim what has no connection to the religion, as there exists today among the crafts, in engineering, medicine, agriculture, warfare, and the like.

Many learners multiplied because of this, until the number of scribes of revelation reached forty-two men. Then the spread of writing came with Islam, and the text on writing for the documentation of religion came in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt with one another for a specified term, write it down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], the verse. It is the longest verse in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, in which the entirety of modern legal documentation is inscribed.

If this is the status of the pen and learning it, then there has been discussion about teaching it to women, on the basis that they are the equals of men in obligation and knowledge. So were they likewise in learning writing or not?

* *

**Topic: Teaching women writing**

Disagreement arose because of two texts on the matter:

The first: the hadith of al-Shifa' bint 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon me while I was with Hafsah, and he said to me: 'Will you not teach her the incantation for the ant-bite, as you taught her writing?'" Al-Majd related it in al-Muntaqa from Ahmad and Abu Dawud, and said after it: "It is evidence for the permissibility of women learning writing."

The second: the hadith of 'A'ishah, which al-Hakim related and al-Bayhaqi authenticated, raised (marfu'): "Do not let them into the upper rooms, and do not teach them writing, meaning the women, but teach them spinning and the Surah of al-Nur." Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar, on the hadith of al-Muntaqa and the hadith of 'A'ishah: the hadith of al-Shifa' is evidence for the permissibility of teaching them, and the hadith of prohibition is to be understood as applying to one for whom there is a fear of corruption from teaching her, meaning teaching her writing and reading.

As for teaching knowledge, it is not a matter of disagreement. The reality is that this question has clear features when you consider it as follows:

First: there is no doubt that knowledge in itself is better than ignorance, and knowledge is of two kinds: knowledge by hearing and receiving. This was the practice of the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and 'A'ishah was the excellent example in this, in the understanding of the Book and the Sunnah. How often did she correct the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and this is well known and established.

Second: knowledge of acquisition through reading and writing. This revolves around whether the benefit exists or not. Whoever sees that teaching them is a corruption prevents it, as was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he passed by a man teaching a woman writing and said: "Do not add evil to evil."

It was also narrated from some of the wise that he saw a woman learning writing, and he said: "A viper given poison to drink." And they recited the following:

*What have women to do with writing, and with office, and with oratory?*
*This is for us, and for them from us is only that they remain in their quarters.*

Similar to it is what al-Manfaluti said:

*O people, the daughters of the world were not created for lessons and for the inscription, and it has been said.*
*For us are sciences, and for them other than these, so teach them how to wash the laundry.*
*And the garment and the needle in her hand are a page upon which every fine line is beautiful.*

He looked at teaching them and their position from one single angle. As another poet said:

*Killing and fighting were written upon us, and upon the adulteresses the dragging of their trains.*

Yet we find in the history of women that women took part in fighting; even 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, used to give water to drink, and Umm Salamah used to treat the wounded, since the statement of neither of them is taken in its generality.

The author of al-Taratib al-Idariyya said: al-Qalqashandi reported that a group of women used to write, and he did not see that any of the predecessors denounced them for it. End of quote.

It is known that Karima related Sahih al-Bukhari, and this is among the reliable transmissions from the muhaddithun. I myself saw, while I was a teacher in al-Ahsa, a copy of Sunan Abi Dawud with the family of al-Mubarak, and on it was an annotation by the sister of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi. The author of al-Taratib al-Idariyya mentioned his statement: "It has been established from many women of the African desert, especially Shinqit (Shinjit, i.e., Shinqit), which is known now as Mauritania, and Timbuktu, and the tribe of Kunta al-'Ajab, to the extent that it is reported that the famous Shaykh al-Mukhtar al-Kunti completed the abridgement of Khalil for men, and his wife completed it in another place for women." End of quote.

What supports what he mentioned is that we, while on the mission of the Islamic University to Africa, while in the city of Atar, which is near the aforementioned city of Shinjit, heard from its elders that there used to be in it previously two hundred girls who memorised the Mudawwana (al-Mudawwana, a major Maliki legal compendium) in full.

I have also heard recently that there was a woman who used to teach in the Prophet's Mosque hadith, sira, and the Arabic language, and she was from Shinqit.

This matter must be looked at in the light of the reality of life today and every day. Teaching women has become one of the necessities of life, but the difficulty lies in the curriculum of their teaching and the manner of their receiving knowledge.

It was therefore necessary that the curriculum of their teaching be restricted to those areas in which it is good for them to work, such as teaching and medicine, and that is sufficient.

As for the manner of teaching them, the difficulty has come only from mixing in university lecture halls and in secondary school classrooms during the period of adolescence, and from scarce supervision. In this lies the danger from them and to them at the same time. So if teaching them is unavoidable, then there must also be a curriculum that achieves its purpose and guarantees safety within it, with success from Allah, glorified is He.

As for what is feared for them from communication through writing, there has been found something closer and faster than it for whoever wishes, which is the telephone in the houses, for it is within reach of the learned and the ignorant alike. The reliance in all of this is upon educational protection, religious firmness, and moral strength.

I have introduced this topic as a digression to explain the viewpoint on this question, drawing from His saying: ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾, and success is from Allah.

* *

**Issue**

Explanation of the priority of writing in general and of Arabic writing in particular, and who first wrote with the pen upon the earth:

It came in al-Matali' al-Nasriyya li-l-Matabi' al-Misriyya, in the original manuscripts printed in the year 1304 AH, the following text: "The foundations of writing are twelve, according to what Ibn Khallikan said, and many authors followed him, such as al-Damiri in Hayat al-Hayawan, and al-Halabi in the Sira and others."

He said: "The writings of all nations, from the inhabitants of the East and the West, are twelve scripts. Five of them are those whose knowers have gone and whose use has ceased, and they are: the Himyaritic, the Coptic, the Berber, the Andalusian, and the Greek. And three of them, those who know them have been lost in the lands of Islam while they are still used in their lands, and they are: the Syriac, the Persian, the Hebrew, and the Arabic." End of quote, summarised; and in it is what is in it.

He said: As for al-Himyariyyah, it is the script of the people of Yemen, the people of Hud, who are the first 'Ad, namely 'Ad of Iram. Their writing was called al-Musnad al-Himyari (the Himyaritic Musnad script), and all its letters were separate (unconnected). They prevented the common people from learning it, so no one practised it except with their permission, until the state of Islam came. Not everyone in all of Yemen could read and write.

Al-Maqrizi said in al-Khutat: "The qalam al-musnad (the Musnad pen) is the first of the pens of Himyar and the kings of 'Ad." End of quotation.

It is now well known that the letters used in writing throughout the entire world, regardless of the spoken languages, are only three: the Arabic script, with the letters alif, ba', and what goes with them, used by the languages of the East; the Latin letters, used by the languages of Europe; and the Chinese characters.

As for languages, there are more than two thousand, "and Amharic with a script close to the Latin."

As for the origin of Arabic writing, the author of al-Matali' al-Nasriyyah said: "The narrations have differed concerning it, as al-Hafiz al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Awa'il."

Likewise in al-Muzhir, in the forty-second type, he said: "He (al-Suyuti) holds that Adam, peace be upon him, was the first to write with the pen, and that all writings originate from him. He had written them on clay and baked it, meaning he burned it and buried it three hundred years before his death. After the Flood, every people found a writing and learned it, and there were twelve writings, and they learned them by divine inspiration."

It is also said: "The first to write in Arabic was Isma'il, peace be upon him." End of quotation.

Al-Suyuti expanded considerably on this question in al-Muzhir, quoting from Ibn Faris al-Shidyaqi.

From al-'Askari, citing the early authorities on this matter, there are several opinions: it is said Isma'il, and it is said Mirar ibn Murrah, and both were from the people of al-Anbar. On this the poet says:

"I wrote Abu Jad, and my hand is Mirar's; I adorned my garment, though I am no writer."

It is also said: "The first to devise it were Abjad, Hawwaz, Hutti, Kalaman, Sa'fas, and Qarashat, who were kings, so the alphabet was named after them."

It is mentioned from al-Hafiz Abu Tahir al-Salafi, with his chain of transmission, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The first to write in Arabic was Harb ibn Umayyah ibn 'Abd Shams. He learned from the people of al-Hirah, and the people of al-Hirah learned from the people of al-Anbar."

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud said in the Kitab al-Masahif: "'Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, who said: We asked the Muhajirun, 'From where did you learn writing?' They said: 'We learned it from the people of al-Hirah.' We asked the people of al-Hirah, 'From where did you learn writing?' They said: 'From the people of al-Anbar.'"

Then Ibn Faris said: "What we say is that writing is tawqifi (divinely taught), and this is evident from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾, and His words: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ [al-Qalam: 1]. And if this is so, it is not far-fetched that Allah should have taught Adam, or another of the prophets, peace be upon them, writing. But that it should be something invented by a person of his own accord, this is something whose soundness we do not know except from a sound report."

Al-Suyuti said: "I say: what supports his view of tawqif is what Ibn Shuqqah narrated through the route of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'The first book that Allah sent down from heaven was Abu Jad.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad, from Abu Dhar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The first to write with the pen was Idris, peace be upon him." End of quotation.

(p-25) He has extended the reports on this matter, of what goes back to the earliest authorities, but there is no sound report in it on which one can rely with certainty.

We have quoted this brief passage specifically for the words of Ibn Faris, that the teaching of writing is a matter of tawqif, and what al-Suyuti cited concerning "the first book that Allah sent down from heaven." Indeed, the Qur'an contains what witnesses to the possibility of this, namely that Allah the Exalted sent down the scriptures to Musa in written form.

And in the hadith: "Allah wrote the tablets for Musa with His own hand, and planted the Garden of Eden with His own hand."

Since Musa received written tablets, the writing must have been known to him before they were sent down, otherwise he would not have recognised them.

As for the most famous of the letters with which we write now, as al-Suyuti said in al-Muzhir, and as the author of al-Matali' al-Misriyyah quoted from him, the text is:

"The well-known view among the people of knowledge is what Ibn al-Kalbi narrated from 'Awanah, who said: 'The first to write with this script of ours was Murar ibn Murrah, Aslam ibn Sidrah, and 'Amir ibn Hadrah,' as in al-Qamus. They were from the Arab tribe of Tayy, who learned it from the scribes of revelation of our master Hud, peace be upon him. Then they taught it to the people of al-Anbar, and from them writing spread in Iraq, al-Hirah and elsewhere. Bishr ibn 'Abd al-Malik, brother of Ukaydir ibn 'Abd al-Malik, lord of Dumat al-Jandal, learned it, and he had companionship with Harb ibn Umayyah, so Harb learned from him. Then Bishr travelled with him to Mecca, and he married al-Sahba' daughter of Harb, sister of Abu Sufyan. A group of the people of Mecca learned from him.

By this, many of the Quraysh who could write in Mecca increased before Islam."

Therefore a Kindite man of the people of Dumat al-Jandal said, reminding the Quraysh of this favour:

"Do not deny the blessing of Bishr upon you, for he was blessed in his fortune and radiant.
He brought you the script of al-Jazm until you preserved from wealth what had been scattered in disorder.
He perfected for you what had been neglected of wealth, and secured for you what had been split apart.
So you set the pens in motion, both in beginning and in return, and you rivalled the scribes of Kisra and Caesar.
And he made you independent of a Musnad ascribed to Himyar, and of what the pens of Himyar inscribed in the scrolls."

He said: Likewise al-Nawawi mentioned in his commentary on Muslim, transmitting from al-Farra', that he said: "They wrote riba in the Mushaf with a waw, because the people of the Hijaz learned writing from the people of al-Hirah, and their dialect pronounced it ribawa, so they taught them the form of the letters according to their dialect." End of quotation.

(p-26) Another note:

His words, the Exalted: ﴿He who taught by the pen﴾, do not prevent His teaching without the pen, as in the story of al-Khidr with Musa, peace be upon him, in His words, the Exalted: ﴿So they found a servant of Ours, to whom We had given mercy from Us, and whom We had taught knowledge from Our presence﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

And as in the hadith: "The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has completed its provision and its term," the hadith in full.

And as in the hadith of the ruqyah with al-Fatihah for the one stung by a scorpion, in the well-known story of the expedition, when the Prophet ﷺ asked him: "How did you know that it was a ruqyah?" He said: "A thing breathed into my heart."

And the hadith of 'Ali, when he was asked, "Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ single you out with any knowledge?" He said: "No, except an understanding which Allah gives to whomever He wills in His Book, and what is in this sheet."

And His words: ﴿Fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

We ask Allah for knowledge of what we do not know, and for acting upon what we know. And success is from Allah.

The Almighty said: ﴿Nay! Surely man transgresses﴾ ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾. The apparent meaning of this verse is that self-sufficiency (istighna') causes transgression (tughyan) in a person. The word "man" (al-insan) here is general, but we find that some people become self-sufficient and do not transgress. This is therefore a case of the general term that has been specified ('amm makhsus, a general expression restricted by a qualifier), and its specifier is either from within the verse itself or from outside it.

Within the verse itself, there is what is indicated by the Almighty's words, ﴿when he sees himself﴾, meaning: when a person sees himself (as self-sufficient). This may be a mistaken view, while the reality is otherwise, and he still transgresses. In that case, self-sufficiency is not the cause of transgression.

For this reason, the Sunnah condemned the arrogant poor man ('a'il mutakabbir), because despite his poverty he sees himself as self-sufficient. He is blamed for his own state, not because of his wealth.

As for what is outside the verse, this meaning is indicated by the Almighty's words: ﴿But as for one who transgressed﴾ ﴿and preferred the worldly life﴾ ﴿indeed, Hellfire will be his refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:37–39]. Preferring the worldly life is what necessitates transgression. Likewise is His saying: ﴿who gathers wealth and counts it﴾ ﴿thinking that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ ﴿No!﴾ and the rest of the verse [al-Humazah 104:2–4].

Its implication (mafhum) is that whoever does not prefer the worldly life and does not think that his wealth will make him immortal, his wealth will not make him transgress, nor will his self-sufficiency, as came in the story of the three men of the Children of Israel: the blind man, the leper, and the bald man.

The Qur'an has explicitly mentioned the greatest worldly wealth in the case of the Prophet of Allah Sulayman (peace be upon him). Allah gave him a kingdom that would not be given to anyone after him, yet he said: ﴿Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord until the sun was hidden by the veil﴾ ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ and the rest of the verse [Sad 38:32].

As for the story of the Companion found in the Muwatta' (of Imam Malik): when he was occupied with his orchard during prayer, upon seeing a bird that could not find an opening among the branches through which it could pass, he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have been tempted by my orchard during my prayer, so it is for the sake of Allah." Thus we know that wealth alone does not necessitate transgression, but when it is accompanied by the preference of the worldly life over the Hereafter. The self's transgression may be one of its inherent qualities even if there were no wealth: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a commander of evil﴾ [Yusuf 12:53]. And nothing protects from this except refinement through religion, as the Almighty said: ﴿If Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely transgress upon the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ and the rest of the verse [al-Shura 42:27].

This was confirmed of Pharaoh when he said: ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:51]. Likewise Qarun said: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 28:78]. And the third of the three men of the Children of Israel said: "I inherited it from elder to elder." This is in contrast to the Muslim, and so on to the end of it. So his wealth does not increase him in anything except humility and gratitude for the blessing, as the Prophet of Allah Sulayman said: ﴿This is from the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself; and whoever is ungrateful - indeed, my Lord is Free of need and Generous﴾ [al-Naml 27:40]. In the same surah it is explicitly stated that he thanked Allah: ﴿So he smiled, amused at her speech, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents and to do righteousness of which You will approve. And admit me by Your mercy into [the ranks of] Your righteous servants"﴾ [al-Naml 27:19].

In general terms, there is His saying: ﴿until, when he reaches maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness of which You will approve. And make righteous for me my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:15].

Among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were some who owned abundant wealth, yet it only increased them in nearness to Allah, such as 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and their like. In the verse there is a subtle connection (rabt latif) with the beginning of the surah, since He created man from a clinging clot ('alaq). That is the state in which he is most in need of Allah's subtle kindness, care, and mercy in his mother's womb. Then it becomes a lump of flesh, then bones, then it is clothed with flesh, then it is brought forth as another creation. Then he comes into this world as an infant who owns nothing but crying. Allah makes two rivers of his mother's milk flow for him, then makes his teeth grow, and opens his intestines. Then he grows up and becomes a youth in his prime. When his Lord tests him with something of wealth or health, he forgets all that preceded, forgets even his Lord, transgresses, and oversteps his limit, even against Allah, his Creator and Provider. The Almighty responded to him with His saying: ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a sperm-drop; and then he is an open adversary?﴾ ﴿And he presents for Us an example and forgets his [own] creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time"﴾ and the rest of the verse [Ya-Sin 36:77–79].

Among the subtle expressions in the verse is His saying: ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾. That is, the transgression into which he falls comes from an illusion, in which he imagines himself self-sufficient, whether by his wealth or by his strength. For the reality of wealth, even if it were mountains, is for him only what he eats, wears, and spends.

Can he eat a single morsel except by the blessing of health? If he falls ill, what benefit is his wealth to him? And if he eats it, does he benefit from it except by a blessing from Allah upon him?

From this verse some people derived that the wealthy thankful person is greater than the poor patient person, because wealth necessitates transgression.

Some people have also said: patience in health is harder than patience in need.

The Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and him, said, in removing the appearance of inconsistency:

﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ يَنْتَهِ لَنَسْفَعًا بِالنّاصِيَةِ﴾ ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ ("If he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinning forelock.")

He attributed the lying to the forelock (nasiyah), while in other places he attributed it to something other than the forelock, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّما يَفْتَرِي الكَذِبَ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ وأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الكاذِبُونَ﴾ ("Only those who do not believe in the signs of God invent falsehood, and they are the liars") [al-Nahl: 105].

He mentioned the answer: that he used "the forelock" and meant its owner, by way of the figure of speech in which a part is mentioned and the whole is intended. He cited Qur'anic evidence for it, such as His saying: ﴿تَبَّتْ يَدا أبِي لَهَبٍ وتَبَّ﴾ ("Perished are the hands of Abu Lahab, and perished he") [al-Masad: 1].

What should be pointed out from the standpoint of eloquence (balaghah) is this: a part that is mentioned and intended to stand for the whole must carry some added distinction suited to the meaning the speech is directed toward.

Here, for example, the passage censures lying and seizes the liar for his lie. The mention of the forelock, which is the front of the hair of the head, came because it is the most disgraceful to its owner and the most humiliating for him, since truthfulness raises the head while lying bows it down in abasement and disgrace.

Thus the forelock is here more fitting than the hand or anything else. In the case of Abu Lahab, the concern was his wealth, with which he acted arrogantly, and the aim is to blame his wealth and his earnings by which he was arrogant. The hand is the organ of earning and the instrument of disposing of wealth, so the hand was more appropriate there than the forelock.

Likewise, they say: بَثَّ الأمِيرُ عُيُونَهُ ("the commander dispatched his eyes"), meaning his spies, because the eye is the most important part of a person for that task. They did not say بَثَّ أرْجُلَهُ ("he dispatched his feet"), nor رُءُوسًا ("heads"), nor أيْدٍ ("hands"), because none of these is like the eye in that respect.

Of this kind also are: ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾ ("hearts that Day will be trembling") [al-Nazi'at: 8], and ﴿ياأيَّتُها النَّفْسُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ ("O soul at rest") [al-Fajr: 27].

This is because the heart is the source of fear, and the soul is the seat of tranquility. Moreover, the soul is a part of the human being, and so on.

From this category is also: ﴿واسْجُدْ واقْتَرِبْ﴾ ("prostrate and draw near") [al-'Alaq: 19], where he mentioned prostration (sujud) and meant prayer (salah), because prostration is the most distinctive of its attributes.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 96, verse 16:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-458) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-'Alaq (The Clot)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾, the verse.

In this noble verse, He attributed lying to the forelock of this disbeliever, which is the front part of the hair of his head, although in many verses He attributed lying to other than the forelock, such as His saying: ﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah invent falsehood, and it is they who are the liars﴾ [an-Nahl: 105].

The answer is evident: here He mentioned the forelock and meant its owner, following the Arabic custom of mentioning a part and meaning the whole. This is common in Arabic speech and in the Qur'an. Among its examples in the Qur'an is this noble verse, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [111], meaning Abu Lahab; and His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], meaning what you have sent forth. Among this is the Arabs' calling the watchman an "eye" (ayn). As for His saying "sinful" (khati'ah), it is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have done by mistake﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5], because the khati' (sinner) is the doer of a sin (khati'ah) or sin (khit' with a kasra on the kha'), and both mean sin, as His saying, exalted is He, clarifies: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter a Fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, their killing was a great sin﴾ [al-Isra': 31].

So the khati' is one who sins deliberately, while the mukhti' (one who errs) is one from whom the act proceeds without intention, and he is excused.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 96, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And prostrate yourself and draw near﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 19].

He linked prostration and drawing near to Allah, as He said: ﴿And during part of the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him through the long night﴾ [Al-Insan: 26]. And His saying, describing His companions, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [Al-Fath: 29]. So His saying, ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾, means they draw near to Him, and this clarifies His saying: ﴿And prostrate yourself and draw near﴾.

This is what indicates at first glance that prayer (salah) is the greatest act of nearness (qurbah) to Allah, since the Messenger (ﷺ) was directed to it from the very beginning, as Allah explained in His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45].

And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The closest a servant is to Allah is when he is prostrating."
